segments.narration: About 170 Viking swords carry the same inlaid name. Ulfberht, spelled out in iron letters down the middle of the blade.
They turn up across Scandinavia and the Baltic, forty-four in Norway alone, made between the ninth and eleventh centuries.
Seventeen of them spell it wrong. Was somebody copying a name they could not read, a thousand years before trademarks?
The name is Frankish, so the workshop was probably in the Rhineland. Three of the swords turned up in Volga Bulgaria, far down the Russian river trade route.
And the best blades are not local metal at all: one is high-carbon steel that may have come from Central Asia. A Frankish brand, foreign steel, seventeen bad spellers.

verdicts.claim: Ulfberht swords date from the 9th to the 11th centuries and are found mostly in Fennoscandia and around the Baltic, with 44 from Norway.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: mostly Fennoscandia and around the Baltic; Norway 44, Sweden 17, Finland 14, Estonia 9, Germany 13; infobox gives 9th to 11th centuries.

verdicts.claim: About 17 known examples carry misspelled forms of the name, such as +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records about 17 misspelled examples, including +VLEBERHIT and +VLFBERTH. The narration poses copying as a question rather than a finding, because Wikipedia attributes the misspellings to illiterate smithy workers and treats deliberate falsification as an open question.

verdicts.claim: The Frankish form of the name points to a Rhineland origin, and three Ulfberht swords were found in Volga Bulgaria, then part of the Volga trade route.

verdicts.claim: One Ulfberht example appears to have been made from high-quality hypereutectoid steel possibly imported from Central Asia.
